content: For individuals presenting with symptoms of vaginal discharge, it is recommended to provide treatment for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and/or Trichomonas vaginalis during the same clinical visit. If molecular testing with quality-assured assays is available, treatment should be based on the results of these tests. In settings where same-day molecular testing is not feasible or where molecular testing is limited or unavailable, treatment should be guided by quality-assured rapid point-of-care tests or syndromic management. Good clinical practice for managing vaginal discharge includes the following steps: Obtain a detailed medical and sexual history and assess the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Conduct a thorough physical examination, including abdominal and pelvic examinations, to evaluate for pelvic inflammatory disease, surgical conditions, or pregnancy. Perform an external vulvovaginal examination to identify any lesions, overt genital discharge, vulval erythema, or excoriations. Perform a bimanual digital vaginal examination to assess for cervical motion tenderness or pelvic pain, which may indicate pelvic inflammatory disease. Additionally, evaluate the presence, color, and consistency of vaginal discharge on the glove. Offer testing for HIV and syphilis, as well as other preventive services, in accordance with relevant guidelines. In settings with access to quality-assured molecular assays and same-day results: 1. Treatment for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and/or T. vaginalis should be based on the results of molecular assays performed on self-collected or clinician-collected vaginal swabs or urine specimens. 2. Treatment for bacterial vaginosis should be considered if vaginal discharge is present (e.g., tenacious or thin) or based on microscopy results, if available. 3. Treatment for candidiasis should be provided if indicated by the type of discharge (e.g., curd-like with vaginal itching) or microscopy findings, if available. In settings where same-day molecular testing is not feasible or molecular testing is limited: 1. Treatment should be guided by quality-assured rapid tests with a minimum sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 90%, if available, to confirm or exclude infections with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. 2. If rapid tests or molecular assays are unavailable, a speculum examination should be performed. Treatment for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be provided if cervicitis is evident. For individuals with negative speculum findings but at high risk of infection, rapid tests or molecular assays should be performed, and treatment should be based on test results. 3. If neither rapid tests nor speculum examinations are feasible or acceptable, individuals at high risk of STIs or those with vaginal discharge on genital examination should be treated for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. 4. Treatment for bacterial vaginosis and T. vaginalis should be provided if vaginal discharge is present or based on microscopy results, if available. 5. Treatment for candidiasis should be provided if indicated by the type of discharge or microscopy findings. For individuals with recurrent or persistent vaginal discharge, referral to a center with laboratory capacity to diagnose infections such as N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, T. vaginalis, and bacterial vaginosis is recommended. Testing for antimicrobial-resistant N. gonorrhoeae and M. genitalium should also be performed if available. If such testing is not accessible in primary care settings, referral to an STI expert, physician, or gynecologist is advised. Microscopy remains the most accurate diagnostic method for bacterial vaginosis and T. vaginalis, with minimal false treatments and less than 1% of cases missed. However, the cost of implementing microscopy in settings without existing facilities outweighs the cost of empirically treating all individuals with confirmed vaginal discharge for bacterial vaginosis and T. vaginalis. The harm to individuals unnecessarily treated (approximately 40%) is considered acceptable given the low cost of treatment. Performing molecular assays for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, or T. vaginalis and basing treatment on these results ensures the highest accuracy in treatment when provided on the same day. Using low-cost rapid point-of-care tests with 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity results in fewer missed cases and unnecessary treatments compared to syndromic approaches or no treatment. Speculum examination combined with microscopy for individuals with negative findings on speculum examination may also reduce missed cases and unnecessary treatments compared to rapid tests alone. Treating all high-risk individuals or those with confirmed vaginal discharge may incur higher costs but significantly reduces pelvic inflammatory disease cases and unnecessary treatments compared to treating everyone empirically.
